title: A brief that starts with purpose
description: Purpose gives a commission brief a useful centre.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Purpose gives a commission brief a useful centre. Begin with what the piece should help someone do, remember or experience before collecting shapes and finishes.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Write one sentence about the intended use and one about why it matters. Add the proposed position or occasion where relevant. Then list the practical questions that could affect the idea. Keep preferred solutions separate so the discussion can consider alternatives.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: “A place for a quiet conversation beside the window” leaves room to discuss form. Starting with an exact table shape may hide that underlying purpose.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A clear purpose does not confirm feasibility, price or availability. It prepares the first conversation.

sections.heading: Choose the next question
paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.

title: Turning ten references into three clear priorities
description: A large reference collection becomes useful when each image has a job.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A large reference collection becomes useful when each image has a job. Reducing ten images to three priorities is an exercise in explanation, not merely deletion.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Give every image a short label describing its useful feature. Group repeated features and identify contradictions. Choose one reference for each leading priority. Retain discarded options privately if useful, but do not send them as equally current instructions.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: Three images might explain outline, colour relationship and placement. A fourth showing the same outline adds less than a sentence explaining why that outline matters.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Can the priorities be explained without the images?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: References communicate direction and do not promise identical reproduction or confirm another maker's design can be copied.

title: Writing a useful list of unresolved questions
description: Unresolved questions are part of a good brief.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Unresolved questions are part of a good brief. Listing them openly helps prevent an assumption from being mistaken for an agreed detail.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Group questions by design, use, material, access and timing. Give each a reason and identify who may be able to answer it. Put the questions that affect other decisions first. Mark answers with their source and date when they arrive.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: If the proposed location is undecided, colour and dimensions may depend on that choice. Resolve the location question before treating either set of preferences as final.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Where will the answer be recorded?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A question list is not a promise that every request is feasible. Some answers may require a revised brief.

title: Separating requirements from preferences
description: Requirements and preferences should be easy to distinguish at a glance.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Requirements and preferences should be easy to distinguish at a glance. This helps a discussion preserve the purpose when a preferred solution is not feasible.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Create separate lists for essential outcomes, preferences and optional ideas. Give each essential outcome a reason. Challenge items that describe a solution without explaining the need. Leave technical feasibility to the appropriate review.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: “The existing doorway must remain usable” describes a constraint. “The object should have a curved end” describes a preferred response that may be reconsidered.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What need sits behind the request?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Labelling a request essential does not prove it can be delivered. Confirm the final design and constraints together.

title: Combining several people's feedback in one brief
description: Several people's feedback is easiest to use when differences remain visible.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Several people's feedback is easiest to use when differences remain visible. Combining all comments into one apparently unanimous instruction can create confusion later.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Collect comments against the same proposal version. Group them by issue and note whether they agree, conflict or need clarification. Choose one person to send the consolidated summary if everyone agrees to that arrangement. Keep unresolved choices explicitly open.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: Two people may both want a quieter design but mean different things: less colour and fewer visible edges. Record both meanings before asking for a revision.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Are comments about the same version?
Who will confirm the consolidated choice?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A consolidated message does not establish consent from people who have not reviewed it. Confirm the summary with the actual decision-makers.

paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.

title: Keeping versions of a reference collection understandable
description: Reference versions need names that explain their status.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Reference versions need names that explain their status. A sequence of files called “final” can make an older idea look current.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Use a short subject, date and version in each filename. Keep a small index identifying the current set and what changed. Mark superseded references without deleting the reasoning they preserve. Avoid mixing personal notes with approved specifications.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: “Entry-console-reference-v03” can be linked to a note saying the colour direction changed while the preferred outline stayed the same.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What changed since the previous set?
Which file records the actual agreement?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A filename is an organisational aid, not approval. The agreed specification must be identifiable separately.

title: Writing a short description before adding images
description: A short written description tests whether a reference collection communicates a coherent idea.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A short written description tests whether a reference collection communicates a coherent idea. It can reveal a missing purpose before more images are added.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Write the intended use, the leading visual relationship and one unresolved question in three sentences. Then attach only the images that explain those sentences. If an image introduces a new direction, either explain it or keep it as a separate alternative.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A description of a quiet hallway focal point may not need a dramatic dining-room image unless a specific detail from it is being referenced.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Can the idea be understood without images?
What question should the atelier answer first?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: The description begins a discussion; it does not book work or replace a quotation and approved design.

paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.

title: What makes a comparison reference useful
description: A comparison reference is useful when the difference being compared is stated.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A comparison reference is useful when the difference being compared is stated. Two attractive images alone may invite the wrong comparison.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Label the alternatives and identify the one feature under discussion. Keep other differences in view as possible distractions. Explain whether you prefer one option or want advice about both. Use a whole-object view if the detail depends on scale.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: If comparing a straight and curved edge, say so. Otherwise a reader might interpret the stronger colour in one image as the main preference.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What answer would move the brief forward?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Comparison does not establish equivalent materials, dimensions or performance. Those may be unknown and should remain so.

title: A drawing legend for separating site facts from proposal marks
description: A drawing legend prevents site facts and proposed ideas from blending together.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A drawing legend prevents site facts and proposed ideas from blending together. This matters when several people add marks to the same image.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Choose simple symbols for measured facts, approximate observations, proposed outlines and unanswered questions. Put the legend on every page. Include a date and author for new annotations. Avoid relying only on colour because printed or shared copies may lose it.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A solid line can mark an existing wall while a dashed line marks a proposed footprint. The legend makes the distinction explicit even in a monochrome copy.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Graphic clarity does not verify the underlying measurements or approve the proposal. Record those statuses separately.

title: A final review of a brief before sending
description: A final brief review should look for contradictions and missing context.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A final brief review should look for contradictions and missing context. It is a preparation step before sending, not an automatic approval of the design.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Read the written purpose first, then check the references against it. Verify names, units, location changes and the current version. Remove private information that is unnecessary for the request. End with a short list of the answers you need from the first conversation.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A reference labelled “alternative” should not also appear under “must have.” Correcting that small inconsistency can prevent a larger misunderstanding.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What response are you asking for?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Saving or sending a brief creates a request. Feasibility, quotation, payment arrangements and delivery require separate agreement.

sections.heading: Choose the next question
paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.
